name: Neutral-Atom Arrays
what: Arrays of neutral atoms held by optical tweezers, notable for scaling to large qubit counts and flexible geometry.
how: Optical tweezers position atoms; Rydberg excitation creates strong, switchable interactions.

name: Superconducting Qubits
what: Qubits built from superconducting circuits cooled to near absolute zero, the most widely deployed quantum processor design today.
how: Josephson junctions form artificial atoms; microwave pulses drive gates inside a dilution refrigerator.

name: Trapped-Ion Qubits
what: Individual ions held in electromagnetic traps and manipulated with lasers, known for long coherence times and high gate fidelity.
how: Ions confined in RF traps; laser pulses drive entangling gates between any pair in the chain.

name: Photonic Quantum Computing
what: Quantum processors that encode information in light, able to operate without dilution refrigerators and integrate naturally with fibre networks.
how: Squeezed light states and interferometer meshes on photonic chips, measured with photon detectors.

name: Silicon Spin Qubits
what: Qubits encoded in the spin of single electrons in silicon, aiming to reuse existing semiconductor fabrication.
how: Gate-defined quantum dots in isotopically purified silicon, controlled electrically.

name: Topological Qubits
what: A qubit design that would store information non-locally so that local noise cannot corrupt it. Still unproven as a working processor.
how: Braiding of quasiparticle excitations in engineered superconductor–semiconductor devices.

name: Quantum Error Correction
use: Turning noisy qubits into reliable ones
what: Encoding one reliable logical qubit across many physical qubits so errors can be detected and corrected mid-computation. The central obstacle between today's machines and useful ones.
how: Stabiliser codes such as the surface code, with repeated syndrome measurement and real-time decoding.

name: Logical Qubits
use: The unit that actually matters for applications
what: Error-corrected qubits assembled from many physical ones. Counting logical rather than physical qubits is the honest measure of a machine's power.
how: Error-correcting codes plus fault-tolerant gate schemes such as lattice surgery or transversal gates.

name: Real-Time Error Decoders
use: Keeping correction ahead of error accumulation
what: Classical hardware that interprets error syndromes fast enough to correct a running quantum computation, a prerequisite for fault tolerance.
how: FPGA and ASIC decoders running matching or neural-network algorithms within the qubit coherence window.

name: Magic State Distillation
what: A procedure to produce the high-quality resource states needed for the gates error-correcting codes cannot perform directly. A major driver of total qubit cost.
how: Many noisy resource states are consumed to distil fewer, cleaner ones.

name: Quantum Advantage Benchmarks
use: Measuring real progress against classical computers
what: Experiments claiming a quantum machine outperformed classical simulation on a specific task. Several have later been matched by improved classical algorithms, so each claim is provisional.
how: Random circuit sampling and boson sampling, checked against the best classical simulations.

name: Quantum Optimisation Algorithms
what: Algorithms that search for good solutions to hard combinatorial problems. Real-world advantage over the best classical methods remains unproven.
how: Variational circuits (QAOA) and quantum annealing schedules.

name: Quantum Simulation of Chemistry
what: Using quantum computers to model molecules and materials whose electron correlations are intractable classically — the application most experts expect to deliver value first.
how: Hamiltonian simulation and phase estimation on error-corrected hardware.

name: Shor's Algorithm
what: The algorithm that would break today's public-key cryptography by factoring large numbers efficiently. Requires far more error-corrected qubits than any machine now has.
how: Quantum period finding via the quantum Fourier transform.

name: Quantum Machine Learning
what: Machine-learning methods running on quantum hardware. Clearest theoretical benefit is for data that is itself quantum; claims of broad speedups on classical data are contested.
how: Parameterised quantum circuits trained with classical optimisers; quantum kernel methods.

name: Optical Atomic Clocks
what: Clocks referenced to optical atomic transitions, precise enough that relativistic time dilation is measurable over small height differences.
how: Ultra-stable lasers locked to narrow transitions in trapped atoms or ions.

name: Quantum Sensing
what: Measurement devices exploiting quantum states to beat classical sensitivity limits — the nearest-term commercial quantum technology.
how: Atom interferometers, NV-centre magnetometers and squeezed-light readout.

name: NV-Centre Magnetometry
what: Diamond defect centres used as magnetic-field sensors that work at room temperature and at very small scales.
how: Optically detected magnetic resonance of nitrogen-vacancy centres in diamond.

name: Quantum Gravimetry
what: Gravity sensors using falling cold atoms, able to map buried structures and voids without excavation.
how: Atom interferometers measure acceleration of free-falling atomic clouds.

name: Quantum Key Distribution
what: Distributing encryption keys using quantum states, where interception disturbs the signal and is detected. Deployed on metro fibre links and satellite demonstrations.
how: Single-photon or continuous-variable protocols such as BB84 over fibre or free space.

name: Quantum Repeaters
use: Extending quantum links beyond fibre loss limits
what: Devices that extend entanglement across long distances without measuring the signal, the missing piece for a wide-area quantum network.
how: Entanglement swapping between memory nodes, with purification to restore fidelity.

name: Quantum Internet
what: A network distributing entanglement between distant quantum processors, enabling tasks no classical network can perform. Early multi-node testbeds exist; wide deployment does not.
how: Quantum memories, repeaters and entanglement-distribution protocols over fibre and satellite.

name: Harvest-Now-Decrypt-Later Risk
what: The risk that encrypted traffic captured today is stored until a future quantum computer can decrypt it — which makes migration urgent for data that must stay secret for years.
how: Mitigated by migrating long-lived secrets to post-quantum algorithms now.

name: Post-Quantum Cryptography
use: Protecting data against future quantum attack
what: Classical encryption algorithms designed to resist quantum attack, now standardised and being rolled out across major platforms — the practical response to Shor's algorithm.
how: Lattice-based, hash-based and code-based schemes selected through the NIST standardisation process.

name: Cryptographic Agility
what: Designing systems so encryption algorithms can be replaced quickly, so the next migration does not take a decade.
how: Abstracted crypto interfaces, inventory of cryptographic assets, hybrid classical/post-quantum modes.

name: Quantum Cloud Access
what: Cloud services giving remote access to quantum processors, how nearly all users reach quantum hardware today.
how: Job queues and SDKs over cloud APIs, often across several hardware vendors.

name: Quantum Software Stack
what: Compilers, transpilers and error-mitigation layers that turn an abstract algorithm into pulses a specific machine can run.
how: Circuit optimisation, qubit routing and hardware-aware scheduling.

name: Cryogenic Control Electronics
what: Control chips that operate inside the refrigerator, addressing the wiring problem that limits how many qubits a dilution fridge can host.
how: CMOS control ASICs qualified for millikelvin operation, multiplexing many qubit lines.

name: Surface-Code Error Correction
what: Two-dimensional lattices of physical qubits encode one logical qubit and correct both bit-flip and phase-flip errors, and several groups have now demonstrated logical error rates falling as the code distance grows. This crossing point is the threshold condition for scalable fault tolerance.
how: A square lattice of data and measure qubits is repeatedly interrogated by stabiliser measurements; a decoder infers the most likely error chain from the syndrome history and applies a correction.

name: Quantum Low-Density Parity-Check Codes
what: Quantum LDPC codes promise a tenfold or better reduction in the number of physical qubits needed per logical qubit compared with the surface code, by encoding information in highly connected high-rate codes. Small-scale demonstrations have already run on trapped-ion hardware.
how: Sparse parity-check matrices define a code whose stabilisers are measured on a connectivity graph; belief-propagation and ordered-statistics decoders recover the error pattern in near-linear time.

name: Quantum Error Mitigation
use: Extracting useful results from noisy hardware
what: Classical post-processing techniques suppress the effect of noise on near-term devices without full error correction, using zero-noise extrapolation, probabilistic error cancellation and symmetry verification. Mitigation buys usable accuracy today while correction matures.
how: Circuits are run at several noise levels and the results extrapolated to the zero-noise limit, or known noise channels are inverted statistically across many sampled circuit variants.

name: Variational Quantum Eigensolver
what: A hybrid approach in which a shallow parameterised quantum circuit prepares a trial state and a classical optimiser minimises its measured energy. It is the leading candidate for extracting chemistry value from pre-fault-tolerant hardware.
how: An ansatz circuit is executed on the quantum processor to measure expectation values of Pauli terms; a classical loop updates the parameters until the energy converges toward the ground state.

name: Quantum Phase Estimation
what: The canonical fault-tolerant primitive that reads out the eigenvalue of a unitary operator to arbitrary precision and underlies Shor factoring and quantum simulation. Its deep circuits make it the benchmark that error-corrected machines must clear.
how: An ancilla register is placed into superposition and controls repeated applications of the unitary to a target register; inverse quantum Fourier transform on the ancilla yields the phase as a binary fraction.

name: Quantum Amplitude Estimation for Finance
use: Derivative pricing, risk analysis, portfolio optimisation
what: Amplitude estimation delivers a quadratic speedup over Monte Carlo sampling for expectation values, the core computation behind derivative pricing and risk aggregation. Banks are running the proof-of-concept work that will define first commercial advantage.
how: A state-preparation operator encodes the probability distribution and an objective operator marks favourable outcomes; amplitude estimation then extracts the expectation with quadratically fewer samples.

name: Optically Pumped Magnetometer MEG
use: Wearable brain imaging, epilepsy mapping, neuroscience
what: Atomic-vapour magnetometers detect the femtotesla magnetic fields of neuronal currents without cryogenics, allowing a helmet the patient can wear and move in. This replaces room-sized cryogenic SQUID arrays in clinical magnetoencephalography.
how: A rubidium vapour cell is optically pumped and probed by a detuned laser; the spin precession rate responds linearly to the ambient magnetic field, which is read optically.

name: Quantum Random Number Generator
use: Key generation, simulation, gaming, certified randomness
what: Devices that derive random bits from the intrinsic indeterminacy of quantum measurement produce randomness that is certified rather than assumed, unlike pseudorandom generators. Chip-scale units are already integrated into security modules and cloud services.
how: Single-photon detection events, vacuum fluctuations or phase noise in an optical interferometer are digitised and processed through a randomness extractor to yield unbiased output.

name: Cryogenic Dilution Refrigeration
use: Cooling superconducting and spin qubits to millikelvin temperatures
what: Dilution refrigerators are the enabling plant for superconducting and many semiconductor qubit platforms, holding mixing chambers below ten millikelvin for weeks. Throughput, wiring density and vibration isolation are now system-level constraints on qubit count.
how: Helium-3 and helium-4 are mixed and separated in a continuous cycle; the enthalpy of mixing across the phase boundary absorbs heat and cools the mixing chamber without moving parts in the cold stage.

name: Quantum Annealing
what: Special-purpose quantum processors that settle a network of qubits into a low-energy state encoding the answer to an optimisation problem, rather than running gate-based circuits.
how: Qubits start in superposition under a strong transverse field that is slowly reduced, letting the system settle toward the problem Hamiltonian ground state.

name: Grover's Algorithm
what: Grover's algorithm searches an unsorted space in square-root time, the canonical quadratic speedup underlying quantum approaches to unstructured search, constraint satisfaction and symmetric-key cryptanalysis.
how: An oracle marks the target state with a phase flip; repeated Grover iterations rotate amplitude toward the marked state, and after roughly the square root of N iterations a measurement returns the answer with high probability.

name: HHL Linear Systems Algorithm
what: The Harrow-Hassidim-Lloyd algorithm solves sparse linear systems with exponential scaling advantage in the matrix dimension, the primitive behind many proposed quantum machine-learning and optimisation speedups.
how: Quantum phase estimation writes the matrix eigenvalues into an ancilla register; a controlled rotation inverts each eigenvalue and the register is uncomputed, leaving the solution vector encoded in the amplitudes of the system qubits.

name: Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm
what: QAOA is a variational near-term algorithm that approximates combinatorial optimisation problems as alternating cost and mixer operations on a gate-based device, without requiring full fault tolerance.
how: Parameters of the cost and mixer layers are tuned by a classical optimiser against measured expectation values; circuit depth and parameter choice trade solution quality against noise on the available hardware.

name: Measurement-Based Quantum Computing
what: Instead of executing a gate sequence, this model prepares a large entangled cluster state and computes by measuring its qubits one at a time, making it attractive for photonic hardware where two-qubit gates are probabilistic.
how: A cluster state is generated by entangling many qubits; adaptive single-qubit measurements with classical feed-forward of outcomes implement any circuit, consuming the entanglement as the computation proceeds.

name: Bosonic Cat Qubits
what: Qubits encoded in superpositions of coherent states of a microwave resonator are intrinsically biased against bit-flip errors, giving a hardware-level advantage that simplifies the error-correction stack.
how: A nonlinear element stabilises two coherent states of opposite phase inside the cavity; photon loss causes predominantly phase flips, so a cheap repetition code corrects the dominant error channel while bit flips remain exponentially suppressed.

name: Fluxonium Qubits
what: Fluxonium circuits trade the transmon's simple control scheme for much longer coherence times and larger anharmonicity, improving the fidelity of two-qubit gates and reducing leakage to higher levels.
how: A Josephson junction shunted by a large superinductance produces a heavy, well-localised wavefunction insensitive to charge noise, with transitions driven at lower frequencies than a comparable transmon.

name: GKP Bosonic Codes
what: Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill codes encode a logical qubit in a periodic grid of oscillator states, correcting both bit and phase flips within a single bosonic mode and enabling hardware-efficient error correction.
how: A microwave cavity is driven into a lattice of squeezed states; small displacement errors shift the lattice and are detected and corrected by measuring stabiliser displacements without collapsing the encoded logical information.

name: Quantum Memory
what: A quantum memory stores an unknown quantum state and releases it on demand with fidelity above the classical limit, the missing component for synchronising nodes in a quantum network.
how: Rare-earth-doped crystals or cold atomic ensembles absorb a photon into a collective excitation, hold it using spin echoes or dynamical decoupling, and re-emit it after a controllable delay.

name: Microwave-to-Optical Transduction
what: Superconducting qubits operate at microwave frequencies that attenuate rapidly in optical fibre, so a device converting single photons between microwave and telecom wavelengths is essential for linking quantum processors over distance.
how: Electro-optic or optomechanical devices couple a microwave cavity to an optical cavity so that a single microwave photon shifts the optical resonance, transferring the quantum state without adding thermal noise.
companies: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)

name: Quantum Illumination
what: Quantum illumination uses entangled photon pairs to detect a weakly reflecting target against a bright thermal background with fewer measurements than any classical radar operating at the same power.
how: One photon of each pair probes the target while its twin is retained locally; coincidence measurements between the returned and retained photons reveal the target even when the idler-target correlation is too faint to detect in either arm alone.

name: Squeezed-Light Interferometry
what: Injecting squeezed vacuum into a laser interferometer suppresses photon shot noise below the vacuum limit, directly extending the reach of gravitational-wave detectors into a larger volume of the universe.
how: A nonlinear optical parametric amplifier squeezes the phase-dependent uncertainty of the vacuum field; injecting it into the interferometer's dark port reduces noise in the measured quadrature at the cost of increased noise in the conjugate one.

name: Quantum-Enhanced Clock Networks
what: Linking optical clocks through fibre networks enables relativistic geodesy, searches for dark-matter couplings and a future redefinition of the second based on an optical transition.
how: Optical frequency combs convert clock signals to telecom wavelengths for fibre transport; comparing clocks at distant sites measures gravitational potential differences and slow drifts at centimetre and nanohertz sensitivity.
companies: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)

name: Quantum Control Electronics
what: Generating, timing and digitising the analogue signals that drive thousands of qubits is a scaling bottleneck second only to fabrication. Rack-mount and cryo-CMOS control stacks now target hundreds of channels per unit with picosecond synchronisation.
how: Arbitrary waveform generators and FPGAs synthesise microwave and baseband pulses, while digitising channels capture readout signals, all phase-locked to a shared reference clock.

name: Cold-Atom Gravimetry and Inertial Navigation
what: Cold-atom interferometers measure gravity and acceleration without the drift that limits classical instruments, which matters most where satellite navigation is unavailable. Instruments are already deployed for geophysical survey and are being ruggedised for vehicle use.
how: Atoms are cooled and launched, then split and recombined with laser pulses; the interference phase depends on the gravitational field difference along the two interferometer arms.

name: Quantum Fourier Transform
what: The quantum analogue of the discrete Fourier transform, mapping amplitude from the computational basis into the phase basis in a circuit of depth quadratic in the number of qubits. It is the subroutine beneath Shor's algorithm, phase estimation and many algebraic speedups.
how: Hadamard gates create superposition and controlled phase rotations imprint binary-weighted phases, followed by a swap network to reverse qubit order. Running it in reverse performs phase estimation on an encoded unitary.

name: Quantum Signal Processing
what: A framework that applies a chosen polynomial transformation to the eigenvalues of a unitary using a sequence of single-qubit rotations interleaved with controlled applications of that unitary. It unifies many known quantum speedups under one construction.
how: A phase sequence is computed classically from the target polynomial, then realised as rotation angles in the circuit. The resulting block encoding produces a matrix whose singular values are the transformed values of the original.

name: Quantum Singular Value Transformation
what: A generalisation of quantum signal processing to non-unitary inputs supplied as block encodings, allowing arbitrary polynomial functions of a matrix's singular values to be computed coherently. It subsumes amplitude amplification, Hamiltonian simulation and matrix inversion as special cases.
how: The target matrix is embedded in a larger unitary so it appears as a block. Quantum signal processing then applies the polynomial to that block, and measurement or amplitude amplification extracts the result with provable complexity bounds.

name: Quantum Walk Algorithms
what: Discrete and continuous time quantum walks that propagate amplitude across a graph and achieve polynomial or exponential speedups for spatial search, element distinctness and certain graph problems. They are the quantum counterpart of classical random walks.
how: A coin operator and a shift operator alternate to move amplitude between connected vertices. Interference concentrates probability on target vertices far faster than classical diffusion on the same graph.

name: Lattice Surgery
use: Logical gate execution on surface codes
what: A method for performing logical operations between surface-code patches by merging and splitting them, requiring only local measurements along boundary qubits. It makes logical two-qubit gates compatible with planar nearest-neighbour hardware.
how: Adjacent patches are merged by measuring a strip of boundary stabilisers, creating one larger patch, then split again by measuring in the complementary basis. The parity of the merge and split outcomes determines the logical operation applied.

name: Color Codes
what: A family of topological stabiliser codes defined on three-colourable lattices that supports a transversal Clifford gate set, making certain logical operations cheaper to implement than in surface codes.
how: Stabilisers act on faces and vertices of the lattice, and colourability allows a single-qubit logical operator to be applied qubit-by-qubit. The trade-off is higher stabiliser weight and more complex decoding.

name: Erasure-Code Error Correction
what: Error correction schemes that convert physical errors into detected erasures, where the location of the fault is known. Erasure decoding tolerates a far higher fault rate than unknown-location Pauli errors, relaxing hardware thresholds.
how: Qubits are designed so dominant error channels, such as leakage or spontaneous emission, produce a detectable flag. The decoder then treats flagged positions as blanks and corrects only the surviving unknown errors.

name: Flag Qubit Protocols
what: Circuits that add ancilla flag qubits to detect when a low-weight physical fault would otherwise propagate into an uncorrectable high-weight error during syndrome measurement.
how: Flags are entangled with the ancilla used for stabiliser measurement so that dangerous fault paths flip a flag. If a flag fires, the syndrome is treated as unreliable and the measurement is repeated or corrected accordingly.

name: Fault-Tolerant Resource Estimation
what: The discipline of computing exactly how many physical qubits, gates and runtime a fault-tolerant algorithm needs under a stated hardware error model, including magic state factories, routing overhead and distillation. It is the honest bridge between algorithmic claims and hardware reality.
how: A high-level circuit is compiled to a logical gate list, each gate is costed in surface-code cycles based on code distance, and code distance is chosen so logical error rate meets a target. The result is a floor on feasibility.

name: Atom Interferometry for Dark Matter
what: Long-baseline atom interferometers that search for ultralight dark matter and new forces by comparing phase accumulation in two spatially separated atom clouds. Proposed and funded instruments include MAGIS-100 and the AION programme.
how: Atoms are put into superposition of two momentum states, separated over tens to hundreds of metres, then recombined. A passing scalar field would shift the interference phase in a characteristic oscillatory pattern versus the field frequency.

name: Rydberg Atom Electrometry
what: Sensors that use electromagnetically induced transparency in Rydberg atoms to measure radio-frequency electric field strength and phase with self-calibration traceable to atomic constants, without a conventional antenna.
how: A probe laser and coupling laser create transparency in a vapour cell; the radio-frequency field shifts Rydberg energy levels and alters the transparency peak. The shift maps directly to field amplitude and phase.

name: Quantum Diamond Microscope
what: A wide-field magnetometer that images magnetic fields from biological and material samples with micrometre resolution by reading nitrogen-vacancy spin states in a diamond chip placed against the specimen.
how: Green laser light polarises the nitrogen-vacancy spins and microwave pulses manipulate them; the red fluorescence yield depends on local magnetic field. A camera records the fluorescence so an entire field of view is imaged in parallel.

name: Entanglement Distribution Networks
what: Metropolitan and intercity testbeds that establish and route entanglement between many nodes rather than a fixed pair, including the required switching, synchronisation and purification layers.
how: Each link generates entangled pairs, entanglement swapping joins adjacent links into end-to-end connections, and purification improves fidelity. Control planes schedule requests the way classical networks route packets.

name: Lattice-Based Cryptography
what: Key encapsulation and signature schemes whose hardness rests on the learning-with-errors and short-vector problems in high-dimensional lattices, standardised for post-quantum deployment. These are the primary replacements for Diffie-Hellman and RSA key transport.
how: Security depends on the worst-case hardness of lattice problems, with parameters chosen so that no known classical or quantum algorithm solves them in feasible time. Implementations must also resist side-channel and fault attacks.

name: Hash-Based Signatures
what: Signature schemes built only from hash functions, whose security assumptions are the most conservative of any post-quantum family. They are stateless variants suitable for firmware signing and long-lived trust chains.
how: A one-time signature scheme is combined with a Merkle tree or a few-time signature layer to sign many messages from one public key. Security reduces solely to hash preimage and collision resistance.

name: Cryogenic Wafer-Scale Testing
what: Automated probe stations that measure hundreds of qubit devices on a single wafer at dilution temperatures, providing statistical distributions of frequency, coherence and gate fidelity rather than heroic single-device results.
how: Cryogenic wafer probers bring a cooled stage and high-density probe cards into contact with on-die pads, or use multiplexed on-chip readout so many devices are interrogated per cooldown. Yield maps then drive process control.

name: Quantum-Classical Hybrid Orchestration
use: Runtime integration of QPU and CPU
what: Middleware that decouples quantum circuits from classical control loops so variational algorithms, error mitigation and calibration jobs can execute across cloud quantum processors and classical accelerators as one workload.
how: Circuits are compiled to a target device, parameter updates are computed classically between shots, and results stream back through a scheduler that batches and prioritises jobs against device calibration state.

name: Germanium Quantum Dots
what: Spin qubits hosted in germanium quantum wells, exploiting strong spin-orbit coupling for fast all-electrical control and compatibility with established semiconductor manufacturing, including integration with superconducting resonators.
how: Gate-defined quantum dots confine single holes or electrons; microwave drive on a gate rotates the spin. Germanium's low nuclear spin noise and strong spin-orbit interaction give long coherence with fast gates.

name: Andreev Bound State Qubits
what: Qubits formed from Andreev bound states in a semiconductor weak link between superconductors, offering intrinsic protection against charge noise and built from the same hybrid materials stack as Majorana research.
how: Two superconductors are bridged by a semiconducting channel, creating discrete Andreev levels whose spin and parity states form the qubit. Microwave drive manipulates the states and readout uses a nearby resonator.

name: Trapped-Ion QCCD Architecture
use: Fault-tolerant quantum computing, quantum cloud access
what: A trapped-ion architecture in which ions are physically shuttled between dedicated storage, gate and measurement zones inside a microfabricated surface trap. Ion transport delivers all-to-all connectivity between any qubit pair without SWAP networks and permits mid-circuit measurement and qubit reuse, both of which cut the physical-qubit overhead of error correction.
how: Segmented DC electrodes on the trap chip create moving potential wells; adiabatic voltage changes slide an ion chain between zones while shared laser or microwave beams address the gate region.

name: Thin-Film Lithium Niobate Quantum Photonics
what: Lithium niobate on insulator patterned at sub-micron scale provides strong second-order nonlinearity, gigahertz electro-optic switching and low propagation loss on a single chip. It is the leading platform for squeezed-light generation, frequency conversion and the electro-optic modulators used to bridge superconducting qubits and telecom fibre.
how: A thin lithium niobate film bonded to silica on silicon is etched into ridge waveguides; periodic poling and electrode overlays enable quasi-phase-matched parametric down-conversion and phase modulation.

name: Superconducting Nanowire Single-Photon Detectors
use: Photonic quantum computing, quantum key distribution, quantum networking
what: Nanometre-thin superconducting meanders biased just below critical current detect single photons at telecom wavelengths with system efficiencies above ninety percent, sub-twenty-picosecond timing jitter and dark counts in the millihertz range. They are the default detector for every photonic quantum link.
how: A photon breaks Cooper pairs locally, creating a resistive hotspot that diverts the bias current and produces a measurable voltage pulse read out through cryogenic amplifiers.

name: Quantum Dot Single-Photon Sources
what: Indium arsenide or gallium arsenide quantum dots in photonic structures emit indistinguishable single photons on demand with high purity and near-unity indistinguishability under resonant excitation. They are the leading route to deterministic entangled-photon sources for photonic processors.
how: Carrier recombination inside a three-dimensionally confined semiconductor dot emits one photon at a time, and a micropillar or photonic-crystal cavity channels the emission into a single spatial mode.

name: Honeycomb Floquet Codes
what: A measurement-only error-correcting code defined by a periodically varying sequence of two-qubit measurements on a hexagonal lattice. It reaches the encoding rate and distance scaling of the surface code while requiring fewer physical qubits and no stabiliser preparation, which suits hardware where measurement is cheaper than entangling gates.
how: Each round of measurements changes the code space; logical information is preserved in the invariant subspace of the measurement cycle and errors are tracked with an automorphism decoder.

name: Magic State Cultivation
use: Reducing non-Clifford overhead in fault-tolerant runtimes
what: A protocol family that grows many high-fidelity magic states from a modest supply of noisy ones using Clifford operations and error detection rather than full distillation circuits. It attacks the non-Clifford resource that dominates the space-time volume of useful fault-tolerant algorithms.
how: Encoded states are injected into a small code, grown by code deformation, and filtered by post-selection each round so failures are discarded rather than corrected.

name: Quantum Simulation of Lattice Gauge Theories
use: Nuclear and particle physics, condensed-matter gauge models
what: Digital and analogue simulation of gauge fields on a lattice, targeting real-time dynamics of quantum chromodynamics and gauge models that defeat classical Monte Carlo methods because of sign problems. Results have been demonstrated on trapped-ion, superconducting and Rydberg platforms in one and two dimensions.
how: Gauge fields map onto qubits or qudits with constraint-preserving circuits; time evolution is Trotterised or realised through native analog interactions.

name: Quantum Interior-Point Optimisation
use: Linear and semidefinite programming, logistics, finance
what: Quantum linear-algebra primitives applied to the Newton steps of interior-point methods for linear and semidefinite programming, giving polynomial speedups in problem dimension under block-encoding assumptions. Practical value depends on fast quantum random-access memory and efficient state preparation of the constraint matrix.
how: Each iteration solves a linear system for the Newton direction with a quantum singular value transformation or HHL-type solver, then updates the barrier parameter classically.

name: Quantum Cryptanalysis Resource Estimation
what: Rigorous accounting of the qubits, T-gates and runtime required for Shor's algorithm to break RSA-2048 and elliptic-curve cryptography, used to set realistic migration deadlines for post-quantum standards. Published estimates span roughly twenty million noisy physical qubits for RSA-2048 over eight hours down to well under a million when fast surface-code cycles and magic state cultivation are ass
how: Circuit-level resource counts are compiled through lattice surgery and distillation models against a chosen physical error rate to yield space-time volume estimates.

name: Topological Quantum Gravity Processors
use: Simulate quantum spacetime dynamics for fundamental physics and secure communications
what: Combines topological qubits with emergent graviton modes to perform error‑free computation on curved‑space manifolds.
how: Nanofabricated Majorana‑based qubit lattices are coupled to superconducting graviton resonators; error correction leverages braiding of space‑time defects.

name: Concatenated Quantum Codes
what: Nests an outer code around an inner code so the logical error rate falls exponentially with the number of levels, at the cost of more physical qubits per logical qubit. The approach suits hardware where physical error rates are high and qubit counts are the cheaper resource.
how: Each level encodes a logical qubit into several lower-level qubits and error correction runs recursively, with innermost syndromes decoded first and corrected results passed upward, allowing a small number of fast decoders to service all outer levels.

name: Quantum Algorithms for Differential Equations
what: Quantum routines that solve partial and ordinary differential equations through linear-system formulations, variational ansatze or quantum walks, targeting simulation of flow, fields and derivative pricing where classical discretisation becomes expensive in three dimensions.
how: The equation is discretised into a large sparse linear system, the system matrix is embedded as a block encoding, and a quantum linear-systems or variational routine produces the solution, with a separate readout step extracting the physical quantities actually wanted.

name: Qubit Foundry and Process Design Kits
use: External chip design, multi-qubit wafer production
what: Wafer-scale fabrication lines that build superconducting and silicon-spin qubit chips to a published process recipe, paired with process design kits that let university and startup teams design a chip without owning a fab. Recipes specify Josephson junction deposition, junction area uniformity, resonator geometry and flip-chip interconnect so that a design submitted as a layout file returns as a p
how: Standard 200 mm and 300 mm CMOS-compatible tooling deposits niobium, tantalum and aluminium films, defines tunnel junctions by shadow evaporation or Dolan-bridge lithography, and uses airbridge and through-silicon-via routing for signal escape. Statistical process control tracks junction resistance to hold qubit frequency targeting within a few megahertz across the wafer.

name: Kinetic Inductance Parametric Amplifiers
use: Qubit readout, dark-matter and axion searches
what: Broadband near-quantum-limited amplifiers built from high-kinetic-inductance superconducting transmission lines instead of Josephson junctions, so they tolerate magnetic fields and dissipate almost no heat at millikelvin temperatures. Their wide instantaneous bandwidth lets one amplifier read out many qubits at once rather than one narrow resonator band at a time.
how: A long coplanar waveguide of disordered niobium titanium nitride or titanium nitride carries a nonlinear kinetic inductance that mixes a strong pump tone with the faint signal, producing four-wave-mixing gain near twenty decibels with added noise close to the quantum limit.

name: Cryogenic Wiring and Signal Distribution
use: Dilution refrigerator wiring, qubit control delivery
what: The cabling, attenuators, filters, circulators and flexible superconducting ribbons that carry microwave and digital control signals from room temperature down to the mixing chamber while keeping heat load inside the cooling budget. Poor wiring design, not the qubits, is a common limit on how many qubits a refrigerator can actually operate.
how: Phosphor-bronze coaxial lines are thermally anchored at each cooling stage and heavily attenuated to strip room-temperature noise, while superconducting flexible circuits replace bulky coax bundles so hundreds of control lines pass through narrow still and cold-plate apertures without saturating the dilution unit.

name: Tensor-Network Simulation of Quantum Circuits
what: Classical methods that represent a many-qubit state as a network of low-rank tensors rather than a full exponential vector, giving faithful simulation of structured circuits that resist brute-force and Monte Carlo treatment. They define the moving boundary of verifiable quantum advantage, because any circuit a tensor network can contract is not demonstrating advantage.
how: Matrix product states, projected entangled pair states and gate-fusion variants exploit limited entanglement, low circuit depth and geometric locality. Bond dimension growth controls accuracy and runtime, and contraction ordering is chosen to keep intermediate tensors tractable.

name: Quantum Reservoir Computing
what: A learning scheme that fixes a quantum circuit or continuously driven quantum system as an untrained reservoir and trains only a simple classical readout on its measured observables. Because training touches only the readout, it avoids the barren-plateau and optimisation problems that cripple variational quantum machine learning.
how: Input data is encoded into the reservoir through Hamiltonian parameters or drive amplitudes, the system evolves under its natural dynamics, short-time correlation functions are measured, and a linear regression maps those features to the target output. Performance depends on the fading memory and expressivity of the reservoir dynamics.

name: Quantum Monte Carlo on Quantum Hardware
what: Hybrid algorithms that use phase estimation or amplitude amplification to attack the sign problem and the long imaginary-time projection that limit classical quantum Monte Carlo for strongly correlated fermions and frustrated magnets. They target exactly the electronic-structure regime where classical methods become unreliable.
how: Trial wavefunctions are prepared on the quantum register, imaginary-time or projector evolution is compiled into controlled unitaries, and amplitude estimation extracts ground-state energies and correlation functions with error scaling polynomially rather than exponentially in system size.

name: Nuclear Magnetic Resonance Gyroscopes
use: Navigation without GNSS, submersible and aerospace guidance
what: Compact rotation sensors that measure the precession of spin-polarised noble-gas nuclei to report angular rate with high stability and no moving parts. They are the leading candidate for long-duration GNSS-free navigation because they can hold bias stability over many hours.
how: Laser optical pumping aligns xenon and rubidium spins inside a microfabricated cell, an applied magnetic field sets the Larmor precession frequency, and sensor rotation shifts the precession phase differentially between two isotopes so that the difference cancels field drift.

name: Nanoscale Magnetic Resonance Imaging
what: Magnetic resonance imaging pushed toward atomic resolution by detecting the tiny force or spin signal from a handful of nuclei instead of an ensemble. It offers non-destructive chemical identification with three-dimensional spatial resolution, complementing scanning probe and electron microscopy.
how: A magnetic tip on a cantilever or a nitrogen-vacancy centre in diamond is brought within nanometres of the sample, nuclear spins are polarised, and their dipolar coupling to the sensor is read out as a frequency shift while gradients applied by the tip encode position along each axis.

name: Twin-Field Quantum Key Distribution
what: A protocol that removes the fundamental rate-versus-distance limit of standard quantum key distribution by interfering single photons sent from two distant transmitters to a midpoint detector, so key rate falls with the square root of channel transmittance instead of linearly. It extends secure key distribution toward intercity range without trusted nodes.
how: Alice and Bob each send phase-randomised weak coherent pulses to Charlie, who performs single-photon interference and announces the detection. The senders post-select on matching basis and intensity, and decoy-state analysis bounds the information an eavesdropper could hold.

name: National Quantum Testbeds and User Facilities
what: Shared, publicly funded hardware platforms that give researchers and startups scheduled access to real quantum processors, simulators and control stacks without building a laboratory. They function as the neutral benchmarking ground where performance claims can be reproduced by outside groups.
how: Facilities integrate one or more qubit modalities behind a common job queue, cloud API and calibration service, with open datasets of device noise, connectivity and gate fidelities so results are comparable across submissions and hardware generations.

name: Single-Photon Detector Arrays
use: Quantum optics, QKD receivers, lidar, biological imaging
what: Multipixel avalanche detectors that register individual photons with picosecond timing and position information across a large field of view, enabling photon-starved imaging and high-rate quantum communication receivers. Array scale, not per-pixel performance, is the current frontier.
how: Arrays of superconducting nanowires or silicon photomultiplier cells are read out with cryogenic or CMOS multiplexing that timestamps which pixel fired and when, and time-tagging electronics correlate arrivals against a clock or pump pulse to reconstruct interference and ranging information.

name: Quantum Batteries
use: Ultrafast charging and coherent energy storage
what: Storage in which charging is a collective quantum effect rather than a classical electrochemical one: a set of absorbers coupled to a shared electromagnetic mode charges faster than the sum of its independent parts. Superabsorption and collective Dicke-type charging have been observed in molecular and microwave-cavity systems, but no device yet stores useful energy at useful efficiency.
how: Absorber molecules or superconducting qubits sit in a common cavity so their transition dipoles couple collectively, and the collective absorption rate grows superlinearly with the number of units. Practical devices additionally need long coherence times and an extraction pathway that removes stored energy without destroying the coherence that made the fast charge possible.
